Crime and Punishment is Dostoevsky's monumental psychological novel from 1866. It follows Raskolnikov, an impoverished St. Petersburg student who commits murder to test his theory that extraordinary individuals transcend conventional morality. His descent into guilt, paranoia, and spiritual crisis becomes a meditation on conscience, redemption, and the limits of rationalist justification for transgression. Raskolnikov murders an elderly pawnbroker and her sister to fund his studies and prove his theory of moral exceptionalism. The act becomes psychologically unbearable rather than liberating. Sonya Marmeladova is a virtuous young woman forced into prostitution to support her family. She becomes Raskolnikov's confessor and embodies Christian redemption through suffering. The novel is structured as a psychological cat-and-mouse game between Raskolnikov and Porfiry Petrovich, a clever police investigator who gradually extracts a confession. Raskolnikov's attempted justification—that superior individuals may act beyond morality—echoes Nietzschean ethics and reflects nineteenth-century Russian nihilist movements. The epilogue's redemptive turn toward Christian faith was controversial. Readers divided over whether it represents Dostoevsky's genuine message or a concession to censors. Published serially in The Russian Messenger and revised repeatedly, the novel grew in scope and complexity. Today it stands as a cornerstone of psychological realism, establishing the depths that fiction could plumb. Through Raskolnikov and Sonya, Dostoevsky raises the fundamental question of whether redemption is possible and what form it must take.
